opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to how hard the problem actually is. People sometimes talk about embodied intelligence as if it were the next chapter of large language models: scale up the data, scale up the model, and general capability will just emerge. But the physical world is much less forgiving than text. A robot has to deal with friction, deformable objects, sensor noise, latency and safety, all at once, in real time. No single team today can be world-class at hardware, perception, control, data collection, foundation models and deployment simultaneously.

If you look at how mature industries developed, like automobiles, smartphones or semiconductors, they didn't scale because one company did everything. They scaled because the value chain split into layers. Someone made the best chips, someone made the best displays, someone made the operating system, and the integrators put it together. That division of labor is what drove costs down and quality up. Embodied intelligence is still at a stage where many companies try to be full-stack, partly out of necessity, because the supply chain isn't mature yet. But that's very capital-intensive, and it spreads talent thin.

There's also a data reason. In embodied AI, data is the scarcest resource, and it's very tied to specific embodiments and scenarios. If every company collects its own small dataset on its own hardware, we end up with lots of fragmented islands. Specialization lets some players focus on producing high-quality, standardized data or infrastructure, so others can build on top of it instead of reinventing it.

Finally, there's commercialization. Customers don't pay for "general intelligence"; they pay for a task done reliably, whether that's sorting packages in a warehouse, loading machines in a factory, or helping in elder care. Each of those needs deep understanding of the scenario. Companies that specialize in a vertical can actually close the loop: deploy, get real feedback, improve, and generate revenue. That revenue and real-world data then feed back into the whole ecosystem.

So to me, specialization isn't the opposite of pursuing generality. It's how the industry gets there. Each layer gets really good at what it does, the interfaces between them become clearer, and over time those pieces come together into something much more general than any single company could build alone.

r001.rationale: The response describes the difficulty of real-time robotics and lists hardware, perception, and control, but does not identify the need to invent both a new physical platform and an L4- or L5-level autonomy stack.

r002.rationale: It says no single team can be world-class across several areas, supporting specialization generally, but does not make the specific argument that one company is unlikely to develop both a new physical platform and the required autonomy stack.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think specialization is necessary because embodied intelligence is simply too big a problem for any single company to solve end to end, at least at this stage.

Look at what a working robot actually requires. You need hardware: actuators, dexterous hands, sensors, the body itself. You need the foundation model, the brain that understands the world and plans actions. You need the data pipeline, whether that's teleoperation, simulation, or real-world deployment data. And then you need the application layer, actually getting the thing into a factory or a warehouse or a home and making it useful. Each of those is a deep discipline on its own. A team that is world-class at motor design is almost never world-class at training large models, and vice versa.

The comparison I keep coming back to is the PC industry, or later the smartphone industry. Nobody won by doing everything. Intel did chips, Microsoft did the operating system, and a whole ecosystem of OEMs did the assembly and distribution. That division of labor is what let the whole industry move fast. In robotics right now, a lot of companies are trying to be Intel, Microsoft, and Dell at the same time, and the result is that they're mediocre at all three and burning capital very quickly.

There's also a data argument. The biggest bottleneck in embodied intelligence isn't compute, it's data. Real-world interaction data is scarce and expensive. If every company insists on its own closed hardware stack, the data never aggregates. Specialization lets you have a few hardware platforms that many model teams can build on, and that's how you get the scale of data that actually produces generalization.

And frankly, there's a talent reality. The people who can do frontier model research are extremely rare. Spreading that talent across fifty vertically integrated companies, each doing a little bit of everything, is a waste. Concentrating it in a few places that focus purely on the brain, and letting other teams focus purely on the body or the deployment, gets you further.

I'm not saying vertical integration never works. At some point, like Apple, someone will integrate it all beautifully. But that comes after the layers mature. Right now we're in the phase where each layer still needs to be invented, and you invent faster when you focus.

r001.rationale: The response lists robot hardware and software layers, but does not say that embodied intelligence requires simultaneously inventing a new physical platform and an L4- or L5-level autonomy stack.

r002.rationale: It argues that one company is unlikely to handle the full problem and contrasts hardware with model development, but does not identify the required combination as a new physical platform and an autonomy stack.

astra-6.text:
I think specialization is necessary because embodied intelligence spans too many disciplines for one company to do everything equally well. You need hardware, control systems, perception, decision-making, and a deep understanding of the environment where the robot will work. Each of those is a difficult problem on its own.

And the requirements change with the application. A robot working in a factory faces different constraints from one working in a home. If you try to address every scenario at once, it becomes difficult to build something reliable and cost-effective. Focusing on a specific task lets you understand the failures, collect relevant data, and improve the system through actual use.

But specialization also needs coordination. The components have to work together, and someone has to take responsibility for the complete system. So I see specialization as a way to build depth while still collaborating closely enough to deliver a useful product.

r001.rationale: The response lists hardware, control, perception, and other disciplines, but does not say embodied intelligence requires inventing a new physical platform together with an L4- or L5-level autonomy stack.

r002.rationale: It says one company may not do every discipline equally well, but does not clearly identify developing both a new physical platform and the required autonomy stack as the reason specialization is necessary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think specialization is necessary because embodied intelligence spans so many different disciplines. You have hardware, sensors, control, learning, and then the practical work of making a robot useful in a particular environment. Each of those areas is difficult on its own. It’s very hard for one company to do everything equally well.

And the requirements change with the task. A robot working in a factory faces different constraints from one working in someone’s home. If you focus on a specific application, you can understand what customers actually need, collect relevant data, and measure whether the system is improving.

But specialization also requires collaboration. The interfaces between components need to be clear so that advances in one area can benefit the whole system. That division of labor is what allows the industry to move beyond demonstrations and deliver reliable products.

r001.rationale: The response lists hardware, sensors, control, and learning, but does not identify the simultaneous invention of a new physical platform and an L4- or L5-level autonomy stack.

r002.rationale: It says one company may struggle to do every area well, but does not specifically connect specialization to the difficulty of developing both a new physical platform and the required autonomy stack.
